title: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} vs {chip:atmel-t5577:name} — The Practical 125 kHz LF Chip Comparison for Access, Cloning, Hotel Retrofit and Migration
summary: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} are the two chip families that dominate the 125 kHz low-frequency (LF) RFID world. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} is read-only — it ships from EM Microelectronic with a factory-burned 40-bit (10-hex-character) unique ID and cannot be re-programmed once issued. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} is the multi-protocol rewritable chip that emulates {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox, Indala, Pyramid, Awid and several other 125 kHz formats; its rewritable memory is precisely why every commodity card-cloning tool ships a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} blank. The chip choice between them is rarely an absolute decision — it is a question of whether the deployment needs read-only durability ({chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}), pre-encoded credential issuance ({chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} or {chip:atmel-t5577:name} once-written), or in-field re-write capability ({chip:atmel-t5577:name}). This page walks through the silicon, the cloning mechanics, the access-control compatibility matrix, the unit-cost ladder and the specific migration scenarios where {chip:atmel-t5577:name} becomes the right answer.
heroPoints: Memory model is the decisive difference. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} ships with a 40-bit factory UID burned into ROM and a 64-bit total memory map; the UID can be read but cannot be re-written. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} carries a full 330-bit configurable EEPROM and a programmable Modulator/configuration register so the same chip can speak {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox 26/35/37-bit, Indala 26/27-bit, Pyramid, AWID and several legacy formats with a single firmware re-write.

Cloning economics are inverted between the two. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} is the format that gets cloned; {chip:atmel-t5577:name} is the chip onto which clones are written. Every $20–$50 commodity 'card duplicator' on Amazon, AliExpress and Shenzhen Huaqiangbei is functionally a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} writer. If your access-control fleet only enforces 125 kHz UID matching, every {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} credential in the fleet is one minute and one {chip:atmel-t5577:name} blank away from being cloned.

Unit-cost delta at volume is small. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} cards land FOB Shenzhen at $0.08–0.15 per card at 50k MOQ; {chip:atmel-t5577:name} cards land at $0.12–0.22 per card at the same MOQ. The 50–80% chip-level price premium for {chip:atmel-t5577:name} is invisible against the headcount cost of re-encoding misissued credentials on the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} read-only platform — but it can still matter in mass-volume programmes (animal ID, hotel-amenity tags, simple proximity badges) where credential personalization is irrelevant.

sections.title: The silicon — what is actually on each chip
sections.intro: Both chips are 125 kHz LF passive devices using ASK / Manchester encoded data, and both work with the same reader hardware. The difference is purely in the memory model and the modulator configuration.
bullets: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} (also sold as EM4102, EM4200 in subsequent revisions) — 64-bit total memory. 9 bits of header, 40 bits of unique ID (10 hex characters, often presented as a 5- or 8-digit decimal Wiegand-26 / Wiegand-34 value), 14 row-and-column parity bits, 1 stop bit. The UID is laser-trimmed at the factory and immutable. No challenge-response, no cryptography, no secondary memory blocks.

{chip:atmel-t5577:name} — 330-bit user EEPROM organised as 7 × 32-bit blocks plus a configuration block. Block 0 carries the modulator configuration register (which protocol to emulate, bit rate, encoding scheme). Block 7 is reserved for the password (if password protection is enabled). Blocks 1–6 carry the actual ID data, padded out to whatever the emulated protocol requires (40 bits for {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, 26/35/37 bits for HID Prox, 27 bits for Indala, etc.).

Read range and reader compatibility are identical — both are 125 kHz ASK Manchester at the air interface, both work with all standard LF readers including HID ProxPoint, ProxPro, Indala ASR, EM-Marin readers, ESP8266 / Arduino DIY readers, Proxmark3 and the entire $20–$50 'card duplicator' commodity tier.

Cost differential at MOQ — {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} wafers are simpler silicon (smaller die, no EEPROM) so they cost less. The cost ladder at 50k card MOQ FOB Shenzhen is roughly {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} $0.08–0.15, EM4200 (re-revision) $0.10–0.16, {chip:atmel-t5577:name} $0.12–0.22, depending on chip-availability cycles and antenna geometry.

sections.title: Cloning mechanics — how a $25 duplicator copies an {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} onto a {chip:atmel-t5577:name}
sections.intro: The reason {chip:atmel-t5577:name} exists commercially is because it is the cheapest way to put an arbitrary 125 kHz credential into a re-writable form factor. The cloning tool reads the source {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, decodes the 40-bit UID, configures the {chip:atmel-t5577:name} modulator block to emulate {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} at the same bit rate, writes the UID into the data blocks and the resulting {chip:atmel-t5577:name} card is indistinguishable from the original to any standard reader.
bullets: Step 1 — Tool reads the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} card by energising its antenna with a 125 kHz field and capturing the ASK-modulated Manchester response. Decode time is under 50 ms.
Step 2 — Tool extracts the 40-bit UID from the response, validates parity.

Step 3 — Tool writes the {chip:atmel-t5577:name} configuration block to emulate {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} (modulator = ASK, bit rate = RF/64, encoding = Manchester, data = blocks 1–2).
Step 4 — Tool writes the 40-bit UID into blocks 1–2 of the {chip:atmel-t5577:name} EEPROM.
Step 5 — Tool reads the cloned {chip:atmel-t5577:name} to verify. Total operation time: 2–6 seconds depending on the tool.
Common commercial tools — Keysy ($35), Handheld Card Copier ($25 on Amazon), Proxmark3 RDV4 ($350 for the pro tier with HID Prox / Indala support too).

Defensive countermeasure on the reader side — Some HID Prox readers (ICLASS SE, multiCLASS) reject {chip:atmel-t5577:name}-emulated credentials by detecting subtle timing differences in the ASK response. This is brittle and not present in commodity readers.

sections.title: When {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} is the right choice
sections.intro: Read-only is a feature, not a limitation, in several deployment patterns.
bullets: Mass-volume single-use credentials — Animal-ID ear tags, hotel-amenity tokens, gym lockers, parking-lot day passes. The chip is consumed once and never re-issued. The 50–80% chip-cost saving compounds at volumes above 250k units per year.

Legacy reader fleets where re-encoding never happens — A 1990s-era HID ProxPoint reader fleet on a single-tenant building has no operational need for in-field credential re-write. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} (or HID Prox on a non-EM4100 chip) suffices.

Anti-counterfeit assistance — When the deployment relies on a factory-issued UID being audit-trailed to a specific batch / customer, {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}'s immutability is a feature.

Animal ID compliance — ISO 11784/11785 Full Duplex/Half Duplex 134.2 kHz is a separate chip family (HDX/FDX-B), but for the older ICAR-registered 125 kHz {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} animal-ID applications, the chip's immutability is part of the regulatory chain.
Lowest-cost simple proximity — When the only requirement is 'reader sees a unique number', {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} hits the spec at minimum cost.

sections.title: When {chip:atmel-t5577:name} is the right choice
sections.intro: Rewritable becomes valuable as soon as the deployment crosses any of these patterns.
bullets: Hotel + multi-tenant retrofit — Where the existing locks are HID Prox or Indala but the customer wants to procure a single chip family for ongoing replenishment. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} lets one SKU emulate the existing format on day one and migrate to a different format later if the lock platform is upgraded.

Pre-encoded credential issuance — The customer wants to ship cards with the credential ID already programmed (e.g., employee badges with payroll-system ID). {chip:atmel-t5577:name} supports this on a Proud Tek encoder line; {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} cannot because the UID is factory-set.

In-field credential rotation — Security-conscious deployments that rotate credential IDs every 90 days. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} allows the re-write; {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} forces a full card re-issue.

Single-SKU procurement across multiple reader formats — A building portfolio with HID Prox in some sites, {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} in others, Indala in a third — {chip:atmel-t5577:name} cards can be configured per site without separate SKUs.

Test / engineering / penetration-test fleets — {chip:atmel-t5577:name} is the de facto standard chip for red-team exercises, capture-the-flag exercises and lab credentials, because any 125 kHz credential format can be staged on a single SKU.

sections.title: Migration patterns and the read-only-to-rewritable upgrade path
sections.intro: Buildings that started on {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and now want {chip:atmel-t5577:name} do not have to flip the entire credential fleet in a single weekend.
bullets: Hybrid issuance — Issue new credentials on {chip:atmel-t5577:name} (emulating {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}) while existing {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} credentials remain in circulation. Both work on the existing reader fleet. Over 12–18 months the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} population attrits out (lost, broken, retired employees).

Reader-side hardening — The harder upgrade is on the reader side. Replacing 125 kHz proximity readers with HF (13.56 MHz, MIFARE Plus / DESFire) readers is the only path to actual cloning resistance. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} only changes the credential medium, not the fundamental 125 kHz cloning surface.

Dual-frequency cards — For buildings starting the HF migration in parallel, dual-frequency cards carry both an LF ({chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} or {chip:atmel-t5577:name}) chip and an HF (MIFARE Classic / Plus / DESFire) chip in the same body. Both readers see the same card during the migration window. Proud Tek's dual-frequency RFID card SKU covers this pattern.

Audit logging — Whatever the credential medium, the meaningful security control is the access-control software logging the reader response and flagging unusual patterns (e.g., the same credential appearing at two readers 200 m apart in the same minute). This is independent of {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} vs {chip:atmel-t5577:name}.

faq.question: Can I tell from looking at a card whether it is {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} or {chip:atmel-t5577:name}?
faq.answer: Not visually — both ship in the same standard 85 × 55 mm PVC body and the antenna geometry is identical. Distinguishing them requires either a tool that reads the chip ID (Proxmark3 will report the chip model on detection) or the per-SKU markings the manufacturer applies. Proud Tek labels every box of cards with the chip family and protocol on the lot label so receiving teams can verify.

faq.question: Will a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} emulating {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} work on every {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} reader?
faq.answer: On every commodity 125 kHz reader, yes. The handful of high-end HID ICLASS SE / multiCLASS readers that perform timing-side-channel rejection of cloned credentials are the exception, and even those can be bypassed by the latest Proxmark3 firmware revisions. Treat {chip:atmel-t5577:name} emulation as functionally equivalent for the 95% of reader fleets in commercial use.

faq.question: Can {chip:atmel-t5577:name} be password-protected to prevent cloning?
faq.answer: Yes — {chip:atmel-t5577:name} supports a 32-bit password lock on the configuration block, which prevents re-writing the modulator config or the data without the password. In practice this is rarely deployed because (a) it does not prevent reading the credential and creating an emulation, and (b) password management adds operational overhead. Password protection is more common in test / lab / pentest fleets than in commodity issuance.

faq.question: Is there a 'secure' 125 kHz chip family that defeats commodity cloning?
faq.answer: Not at commodity price points. HITAG 1 / HITAG 2 / HITAG S add some authentication, but the chips and readers are an order of magnitude more expensive than EM4100/T5577 and HITAG 2 has known vulnerabilities. The practical secure-credential path is to migrate to 13.56 MHz (MIFARE Plus EV2 SL3 or MIFARE DESFire EV3) where {chip:nxp-mifare-desfire-ev3:crypto.algorithm} mutual authentication eliminates the commodity cloning surface entirely. See the linked /compare/125khz-vs-13.56mhz-rfid/ page for the full migration analysis.

faq.question: What MOQ does Proud Tek require for either chip?
faq.answer: EM4100 and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} cards are stocked in standard PVC formats and Proud Tek can ship from 1,000 units. The unit-cost ladder flattens above 50,000 units; below 50,000 units the price ladder steepens because lamination tooling amortises across fewer units. Keyfob form factors carry a higher tooling minimum (typically 5,000 units) but the chip cost is the same.

faq.question: Does either chip work with iPhone NFC reading?
faq.answer: No. Both EM4100 and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} are 125 kHz LF chips. iPhone (and every NFC-enabled smartphone) reads 13.56 MHz HF chips per the NFC Forum specification — not 125 kHz. If smartphone compatibility is a requirement, the chip family must move to 13.56 MHz (MIFARE / NTAG / FeliCa / ICODE).
